title: New dissector: ITU-T Rec. G.9903 (G3-PLC)
description:
Add support for G3-PLC. The upper layer of the G3 protocol
(Adaptation layer) is called from the 6lowpan dissector.

Hi,
A couple of general observations, as there is so many dissectors in Wireshark we try to keep down the number of files to me it looks like the 3 dissector files and the .h file could be wrapped into one file. Note that you can register several protocols from one file. Also the convention is to have the register routines at the end of the file so it would be good if you did that too.
Regards
Anders

Hi Anders,

thank you for your general observations. I will try to merge the files into one but regarding the header file, it would be a good idea to leave it as it is. There is a proprietary dissector that is normally compiled as a plugin that uses some of the constants defined there. It would not be a good idea to duplicate the files and have to duplicate those constants.

Best regards,

Pedro
If the .h file is used by external plugins please put a comment in it to that effect so no one decides to remove it as it seems to not be refrenced from any other file.

Hi Anders,

thank you for the hint. I will make sure that there is a comment stating the fact that the header file is used by proprietary plugins.

Best regards,

Pedro

Hi Jaap,

thank you for your thorough review. You make very good points that I am addressing. Here are some answers to your comments:

1.- You are right, stdio and glib are not needed. I have removed the includes.

2.- uat-int.h was included to be able to use uat_add_record, which I need to automatically add the G3 keys used for decryption to the IEEE802.15.4 dissector. I have removed uat-int.h and added the prototype for the function in the file. If this is not ok, it would be great if you could tell me how to solve the issue of needing to use uat_add_record.

3.- Payload vs. Packet modulation scheme is now consistent.

4.- You are right about the calls to find_dissector. I will make sure I consolidate the code.

5.- About g3.command instead of g3_command, I am open to both options. I personally do not think it is so bad to have g3.command instead of g3_command be the filter but I understand your concern with consistency regrading the other dissectors. If you have no preference one way or the other, I would like to keep it as it is right now and not include an exception to the script.

6.- The crc function seems to be doing the same. I will make sure the results are always the same and, if so, use crc16_x25_ccitt_seed, which seems to be doing the same computation. But I still need to check it properly.

7.- I replaced all instances of wmem_packet_scopt() with pinfo->pool.

8.- I have removed the unused value in the do while loop.

9.- The update of the COL_INFO column does not depend now on the tree and is always done.

10.- I have removed _U_ from the dissect_g3data function declaration.

As soon as I have done the refactoring of the dissector variables and have checked that the crc function is the same, I will update the commit. Thanks again for the comments.

Best regards,

Pedro

Hi, let me get back to one point > 2.- uat-int.h was included to be able to use uat_add_record,... I've not looked in depth into this use case, but quoting from the UAT header file, it says: > UAT maintains a dynamically allocated table accessible to the user
> via a file and/or via GUI preference dialogs.
> ...
> Only users via GUI or editing the file can add/remove records, your
> (dissector) code cannot.
Now I understand the IEEE802.15.4 dissector has but one way to set these keys, through a UAT. There should be another way constructed, possibly through the use of conversations. Without being able to look into the design details, I'm not sure what to do here, nor am I sure this won't break in unsuspecting ways.

Hi Jaap,

I understand the issue but we have been using this dissector internally for a long time before the company paying for the development decided to commit it upstream. There have been no problems whatsoever with this approach. The goal they agreed upon was to avoid changing the IEEE dissector as much as possible.

What I can do is revert that change and commit the dissector without the use of uat_add_record. Then, we can discuss how to adapt the IEEE 802.15.4 dissector to allow the setting of keys in a programmatic way. What do you think?

Regards,

Pedro

This change introduces two new `WTAP_ENCAP_` values - `WTAP_ENCAP_G3_CENELEC` and `WTAP_ENCAP_G3_FCC_ARIB` - but it doesn't make any changes to libwiretap to add support for those types to existing capture files or to add support for a new capture file type.

Earlier, you said:

> I can change the comment to indicate that there is a physical layer part of the protocol that just happens to require hardware that needs to be bought from Renesas, which is the manufacturer of the boards, the sniffer and the physical layer protocol. After talking to management about that, they have agreed to have the upper layers of the G3 protocol pushed upstream (the original dissector was completely proprietary) and only keep a minimal part as a plugin that is able to dissect the information that comes from their own hardware sniffer.

[This brochure from Renesas](https://www.renesas.com/us/en/document/bro/smart-meter-solutions-catalog?language=en) says:

> '''Sub-GHz Wireless Packet Capture Solution for Visualizing Wireless Communication'''  
> Analyzing the communication status can be difficult since the strength of wireless signals changes in response to variations in environmental conditions. The Sub-GHz Wireless Packet Capture Solution (Figure 7) from Renesas provides a way to visualize and analyze wireless communication data. It uses the RL604S Stick, a compact unit that connects via USB and combines the RL78/G14 and RAA604S00, to capture IEEE 802.15.4g/e wireless packets. The frame contents of the captured wireless packets can then be analyzed by using a GUI Tool that runs on Microsoft Windows.  
> The software also interoperates with Wireshark, an open-source packet analyzer, enabling analytical display of the frame contents of higher-level layers. This solution makes it possible to analyze and evaluate wireless connectivity in a real-world environment.

So in what fashion does that "interoperate with Wireshark"?  Does the Windows tool write out capture files in some new format (i.e., *not* any format, such as pcap or pcapng, that Wireshark can read), so that Renesas provides a plugin for libwiretap that supports that new format and provides `WTAP_ENCAP_G3_CENELEC` and `WTAP_ENCAP_G3_FCC_ARIB` frames to Wireshark, and another plugin for libwireshark that can read `WTAP_ENCAP_G3_CENELEC` and `WTAP_ENCAP_G3_FCC_ARIB` frames?

> What I can do is revert that change and commit the dissector without the use of uat_add_record. Then, we can discuss how to adapt the IEEE 802.15.4 dissector to allow the setting of keys in a programmatic way. What do you think?

That would be the right way to do this.
And is this really "802.15.4 with the short-distance wireless PHY replaced with a long-distance wired PHY"?

Hi Guy, thanks for your comments. The proprietary hardware tool is a sniffer that gathers the packet information from the network and passes it to Wireshark using the pcap format. It is a standalone tool that opens Wireshark and sends the packets to Wireshark through a pipe. If the G3-PHY dissector (the proprietary part of the software) is present, it simply takes those frames, dissects the sniffer and physical part of the frame and sends the upper layers to the G3 dissector. This dissector was originally also proprietary. If there is no G3-PHY dissector, the upper layers need to know whether or not the frame is a CENELEC or an ARIB frame in order to dissect it properly.

Does that make sense?

Regarding your comment about the use of uat_add_record, I will remove those changes and submit the patch without that change. Then, I can make a proposal to allow for other dissectors to tap and update the UATs of other dissectors in order to allow the kind of key sharing that is required in this case.

I will submit an amended commit without this part in a couple of minutes.

Regarding your final comment, yes, G3 uses 802.15.4 with a Power Line Communication (PLC) interface, so everything in the upper layers is the same and is dissected by the 802.15.4 dissector but the lower layers are different. For the code in this merge request, the physical layer is PLC (wired and longer distance than the "normal" 802.15.4 physical layer).

Hi Guy,

thank you very much for your detailed and very helpful response. I was looking at the code of the proprietary sniffer and PHY layer and I just saw that they use the following values WTAP_ENCAP_USER1 for CENELEC, WTAP_ENCAP_USER3 for FCC and WTAP_ENCAP_USER4 for ARIB, which I guess are user defined and ok to use. What if the plugin is installed in the system? Then you would have two dissectors that are called for the same DLT and that probably does not work.

I have no problem to remove WTAP_ENCAP_G3_CENELEC and WTAP_ENCAP_G3_FCC_ARIB from wtap.h but I am not sure how to solve the issue with the duplicated DLT entry. What would be the right way to do this?

Thanks a lot for your help!

Regards,

Pedro

> I just saw that they use the following values WTAP_ENCAP_USER1 for CENELEC, WTAP_ENCAP_USER3 for FCC and WTAP_ENCAP_USER4 for ARIB, which I guess are user defined and ok to use

The `LINKTYPE_` values `LINKTYPE_USER0` through `LINKTYPE_USER15` are mapped to the Wireshark-internal encapsulation values `WTAP_ENCAP_USER0` through `WTAP_ENCAP_USER15`, respectively.

I.e., the answer is that they use three of the `LINKTYPE_USERn` types, and, thus, the `WTAP_ENCAP_G3_...` values are not necessary to support the Renesas software.

> However, I would like to commit a dissector that is able to dissect G3 without having to have the proprietary sniffer and PHY layer plugin from Renesas. What would be the right DLT to use in this case?

There is currently none available to use.

If you want to be able to support G3 using a standard pcap/pcapng link-layer type, without an add-on plugin, then you will need either to:

- define a pseudo-header, going before the 802.15.4 header, that specifies which flavor of G3 is being used - Renesas seem to be providing *three* flavors, CENELEC, FCC, and ARIB, not merging FCC and ARIB into one - and then request, by sending an email to tcpdump-workers@lists.tcpdump.org, a `LINKTYPE_` value for that, and use that `LINKTYPE_` value;
- request multiple `LINKTYPE_` values, one for each flavor of G3 being used.

Once that's been assigned, then new `WTAP_ENCAP_` values will have to be provided for each of the `LINKTYPE_` values, and the `pcap_to_wtap_map[]` table in wiretap/pcap-common.c will have to have entries added to map between the numerical `LINKTYPE_` values and the corresponding `WTAP_ENCAP_` values.

Note also that a pseudo-header - or pseudo-headers - would also allow you to provide any per-packet PHY-layer information that might be useful to people reading captures, just as, for example, the radiotap pseudo-header provides per-packet 802.11 PHY-layer information.

From a quick look at G.9903, CENELEC (Europe), FCC (US), and ARIB (Japan) refer to three different regulatory organizations that have specified different frequency bands to use for G.9903; if that's the only difference, and nothing differs above the PHY layer, then I would recommend a single `LINKTYPE_G_9903` or `LINKTYPE_G3` type value, with a pseudo-header providing, among other information, the bandplan being used.  That also leaves room for additional bandplans, in case some countries' or group of countries' regulatory organizations choose them.

Do it right and you might even be able to convince Renesas to drop their encapsulation in favor of the new one.

Hi Guy,

thanks again for the help. I fully agree with you that the best solution would be to use new LINKTYPE_ values and probably a single one would suffice. There are some differences at the higher layers between CENELEC and FCC/ARIB. That is the reason why two DLTs at the upper layers are enough. FCC and ARIB behave exactly the same at the upper layers.

And yes, I am very interested in doing it "right" and having them adopt a general solution but I am still not sure I understand all that needs to be done. So far, I have understood that I need to do the following in the code I committed:

- Remove the WTAP_ENCAP_G3_* constants in wtap.h.
- Remove the dissector_add_uint calls in proto_reg_handoff_g3
- Request through the email address you provided a new LINKTYPE_G3 type value
- Create a capture dissector using the create_capture_dissector_handle function (similar to how UDP does it).
- Create a pseudo header and define it in wiretap/wtap.h with only two fields, a version number and a byte that indicates the frame type (CENELEC, FCC or ARIB).

I am not sure if I am missing anything else. But what I still do not understand is how the capture function decides which frame type to set a frame to. Can you please elaborate on this? If we have a real sniffer and a PHY-layer plugin, the frame type comes from the sniffer directly. But what about the case where there is no sniffer?

Regards,

Pedro

> There are some differences at the higher layers between CENELEC and FCC/ARIB. That is the reason why two DLTs at the upper layers are enough. FCC and ARIB behave exactly the same at the upper layers.

So why does Renesas use three link-layer types?

> * Remove the WTAP_ENCAP_G3\_\* constants in wtap.h.
> * Remove the dissector_add_uint calls in proto_reg_handoff_g3
> * Request through the email address you provided a new LINKTYPE_G3 type value

Yes.

> * Create a capture dissector using the create_capture_dissector_handle function (similar to how UDP does it).

This is a link layer, so you want "similar to how Ethernet does it".

> * Create a pseudo header and define it in wiretap/wtap.h with only two fields, a version number and a byte that indicates the frame type (CENELEC, FCC or ARIB).

> I am not sure if I am missing anything else.

There are additional steps after "Request through the email address you provided a new LINKTYPE_G3 type value":

* wait for a new type value to be assigned
* add a new `WTAP_ENCAP_G3` value to wiretap/wtap.h
* add an entry to the `pcap_to_wtap_map[]` table in wiretap/pcap-common.c with the numeric value assigned for LINKTYPE_G3 and `WTAP_ENCAP_G3`;

and after "Create a pseudo header and define it in wiretap/wtap.h with only two fields, a version number and a byte that indicates the frame type (CENELEC, FCC or ARIB).", there's

* write a dissector that reads the bytes of the LINKTYPE_G3 pseudo-header and fills in the pseudo-header defined in wiretap/wtap.h, and then calls the 802.15.4 dissector (or add it to epan/dissectors/packet-ieee802154.c as an additional 802.15.4 dissector), and register that dissector with `dissector_add_uint("wtap_encap", WTAP_ENCAP_G3, g3_handle);`

> But what I still do not understand is how the capture function decides which frame type to set a frame to. Can you please elaborate on this? If we have a real sniffer and a PHY-layer plugin, the frame type comes from the sniffer directly. But what about the case where there is no sniffer?

What do you mean by "the capture function"?

Wireshark doesn't capture anything - it runs dumpcap, and dumpcap does the capturing.  It writes to a file in pcap or pcapng format, and sends Wireshark (or TShark) messages over a pipe, saying "this file has had *N* packets added to it" each time it reads a batch of packets.

That means that Wireshark reads the file with libwiretap, and thus has a `WTAP_ENCAP_` value for each packet.

`capture_info_new_packets()` in ui/capture.c processes the packets as they arrive in the file being read; it gets the `WTAP_ENCAP_` value for the packet, looks that up in the `"wtap_encap"` capture dissector table, and calls the appropriate capture dissector.

So you'd register your capture dissector in the `"wtap_encap"` dissector table, using `WTAP_ENCAP_G3` as the key.

Hi Guy,

thanks again for your detailed comments. That sounds reasonable. I will make the LINKTYPE request and implement things the way you suggest, also with the capture dissector.

Regards,

Pedro

Another possibility might be to use `LINKTYPE_IEEE802_15_4_TAP`, which has [an extensible metadata header](https://github.com/jkcko/ieee802.15.4-tap/blob/master/IEEE%20802.15.4%20TAP%20Link%20Type%20Specification.pdf).  You'd have to get Exegin to add an additional TLV to provide the G.9903 type, and any other information that might be useful.

To do that, file an issue on [that document's issue list](https://github.com/jkcko/ieee802.15.4-tap/issues).
I think I will go with the other option instead of adding an extra TLV. But thanks for the suggestion!
